subject: Maths
central_question: How can repetition through reflection or rotation be recognised, created, and measured?
in_scope_units: Introduction to symmetry — definite repetition in natural, artistic, and architectural figures
9.1 Line of Symmetry — folding, reflection, multiple lines, and symmetric constructions
Paper cutting, punching, and grid completion — creating reflection symmetry
9.2 Rotational Symmetry — centre of rotation, angles of symmetry, windmills, squares, and radial arms
Comparing reflection and rotational symmetry — figures with one, both, or neither type

known_pitfalls.claim: Every symmetrical figure has a line of symmetry.
known_pitfalls.correction: A pinwheel may have rotational symmetry without reflection symmetry.

known_pitfalls.claim: A non-square rectangle has diagonal symmetry lines.
known_pitfalls.correction: Its diagonals do not make the halves overlap.

known_pitfalls.claim: A 360° return alone proves rotational symmetry.
known_pitfalls.correction: The chapter requires a matching angle strictly below 360°.

recommended_example_progression: Compare the opening flower, butterfly, rangoli, pinwheel, and cloud.
Fold a square to find four lines of symmetry and test a rectangle diagonal.
Use cutting, punching, and grid completion for reflection.
Rotate the windmill and square through 90°, 180°, 270°, and 360°.
ncert_end_of_chapter_exercises_reference: Use the Figure it Out tasks in Sections 9.1–9.2, including regular polygons, Parliament Building, Koch snowflake, Ashoka Chakra, tiles, and the final game.
